Postgraduate MPH Global Public Health Prepare to take on global public health challenges. Gain specialised skills to make a valuable contribution to communities’ health and wellbeing. Our course pages need JavaScript enabled to work correctly. Previous Section Course Overview Next Section Jump to a section Course overview Careers Teaching and modules Facilities Entry requirements Fees and funding Apply Apply now Book on a postgraduate open event MPH Part-time option(s) MPH Start date January 2027 Location Cambridge Award MPH Duration 1 year full-time Part-time option(s) Start date January 2027 Location Cambridge Award MPH Duration 2 years part-time 1st in the region for postgraduates progressing into senior roles. Source: Graduate Outcomes Survey 2026 Covid-19, Ebola, health inequality, conflict, vaccine hesitancy, the role of the state in health. Public health is constantly in the news – and our Master’s degree will equip you to meet contemporary challenges. You’ll take a modern approach, exploring the social, economic and political factors that influence population health. Modules cover the field of public health globally and are applicable to any country or health system. This course will suit you if you’re working in a health-related role and want to take the next step in your career. Faculty of Public Health This Master’s degree is mapped against the Faculty of Public Health training curriculum, supporting professional recognition. Why ARU? Prepare for a career in public health in the UK or internationally Learn about the factors that influence population health Explore public health issues, policies and communication Achieve professional recognition, with a course that maps to the Public Health Training Curriculum Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers Gain the knowledge and skills for a public health career worldwide. Across the globe, increasing demand for healthcare services alongside reduction in funding means there’s a real need for public health professionals. On this course, you’ll cover key concepts including epidemiological research, disease, addiction policy-making and migration, and mental health. As a graduate, you could consider roles in sectors such as health, government, voluntary and community organisations. Graduation doesn’t have to be the end of your time with us. You could choose to continue your academic career with a PhD programme at ARU. Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and save £400 on your fees. How can ARU help with my employability and career development? We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning which may include industry-led projects, placements or Professional Experience modules . Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules Develop your understanding of public health and learn to apply your knowledge to real-world situations. You’ll explore contemporary issues such as infectious disease control, vaccine hesitancy, mental health and migration. Alongside this, you’ll look at local and national policy, health inequalities, and health communication and behaviour change strategies. We’ll prepare you to take on global challenges, as you learn to use demographic statistics and epidemiological data to improve public health. Finally, you’ll plan, design and conduct a major piece of research work with your Postgraduate Research Project. This can be either research- or work-based. What will I study? MPH Part-time option(s) MPH Modules are subject to change and availability, and may vary by location. If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. Year 1 Essential Issues in Public Health and Practice Statistics and Epidemiology Public Health Ethics: Mental Health, Bioethics, and Society Postgraduate Research Project - Public Health Globalisation and Public Health Module details Part-time option(s) It's possible to study this course part-time. You'll take the same modules as MPH students, but sometimes in a different order or in different years. As a part-time student you'll typically study for twice as long as full-time students. For example, if the MPH course takes one year, you can expect to study over two years, though for some courses this may vary. Year 1 Essential Issues in Public Health and Practice Public Health Ethics: Mental Health, Bioethics, and Society Globalisation and Public Health Year 2 Statistics and Epidemiology Postgraduate Research Project - Public Health Module details How is MPH Global Public Health assessed? We'll assess both your theoretical knowledge and practical skills. Assessments have been developed to include skills you'll need in your career such as policy briefs, persuasive arguments, intervention development and written evaluations, debates, and outbreak management plans. Who teaches MPH Global Public Health at ARU? Read profiles of teaching and research staff on this course. Dr Russell Kabir Associate Professor & Course Leader Dr Ali Davod Parsa Associate Professor Clare Jacobs Deputy Head of School Dr Richard Hayhoe Senior Lecturer Dr Lyndsay S. Baines Senior Lecturer in Global Public Health Facilities Enjoy a range of facilities designed to support your studies and career development. These include extensive library and IT resources, and careers support through our Employability Service . After you graduate, you’ll have lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . You can also access support, should you need it, with study skills, health and wellbeing, and more. Please enable JavaScript for "Fees Information" section to function. Entry requirements Standard entry requirements MPH Part-time option(s) MPH A UK Honours Degree or equivalent International students Applicants will be required to demonstrate the University standard of English language (IELTS) at Level 6.5 prior to commencement on a course. Students who do not meet this criterion will be advised to seek support from ALS English language programme prior to commencement of the course. Selection Process Candidates should normally have a good first degree or equivalent and be working, or hope to work, within any area of the public health arena. They do not necessarily need a professional qualification for access to the course but do need to demonstrate a strong interest in public health and local health improvement. Candidates with a third class honours, or ordinary (pass) degree plus a minimum of one year of relevant post-graduate work experience, will be considered on an individual basis. Candidates who do not have a first degree, but have relevant work experience, may be able to gain access to the course by completing a Non Graduate Entry Profile demonstrating, and reflecting on, achievement of generic undergraduate learning outcomes through experiential learning. Admission to the Course with Non-Traditional entry Non graduates may gain entry to the course by clearly demonstrating on their application that their qualifications and experience are equivalent to an Honours degree. Admission with Credit Applicants seeking admission with credit (either APCL or APEL) are referred initially to the AP(E)L Advisor for the Faculty of Health, Education, Medicine and Social Care. Important additional notes Our published entry requirements are a guide only and our decision will be based on your overall suitability for the course as well as whether you meet the minimum entry requirements. Other equivalent qualifications may be accepted for entry to this course; please email [email protected] for further information. Applicants to undergraduate courses can also check our information about undergraduate entry qualifications . You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your course. Part-time option(s) See entry requirements for the MA or MSc International students We welcome applications from international and EU students, and accept a range of international qualifications. See international and EU entry requirements See information about application deadlines You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your course. English language requirements If English is not your first language, you'll need to make sure you meet our English language requirements for postgraduate courses . Check the section ' English language requirements ' for IELTS requirements. Please enable JavaScript for "Fees Information" section to function. We will ask for a deposit of £4,000 or a sponsorship letter Find out about paying your fees . Part-time fees Part-time course fees assume that you’re studying at half the rate of a full-time student (50% intensity). Course fees will be different if you study over a longer period. All fees are for guidance purposes only. Your offer letter will contain full details of credits and fees, or you can contact us if you'd like more information. Source: Graduate Outcomes Survey 2026 Whether you're changing career or expanding your technical expertise, this conversion course in the heart of the Silicon Fen provides a practical pathway into modern data science and AI. You’ll gain hands-on experience in programming, statistics, machine learning, data visualisation, predictive analytics and generative AI through real-world datasets, and graduate with the analytical and technical skills sought by employers across healthcare, finance, business, technology and research. Why ARU? Launch your data science career – no computing or data-related degree required Study and explore career opportunities in Cambridge’s ‘Silicon Fen’, a global hub for tech innovation Build in-demand skills such as data mining, machine learning, statistical modelling and AI Apply your knowledge through hands-on projects using real-life datasets and industry-relevant projects Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers Your mentorship and belief in me have helped me learn and develop skills that I will carry with me for the rest of my career as I start my new role as a data analyst. Merin Mathew, MSc Applied Data Science (Conversion) graduate Gain in-demand skills applicable to a range of careers. This course equips you with highly marketable practical and industry-ready skills needed to thrive in today's data-driven world. You'll develop expertise in programming, data acquisition and cleaning, data visualisation, machine learning, predictive modelling, and artificial intelligence using industry-standard tools and techniques. You'll graduate well prepared for careers in data science, AI, business analytics, healthcare, finance, technology, and research. Graduation doesn't have to be the end of your time with us. You might decide to continue your academic career and join a research programme at ARU. Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and save £400 on your fees. What can you do with an Applied Data Science (Conversion) degree? Organisations and industries increasingly rely on AI and data-driven decision making to solve complex challenges and drive innovation. You might pursue careers in data science, artificial intelligence, business analytics, healthcare analytics, financial technology, cyber security, environmental modelling, smart manufacturing and research. The combination of technical, analytical and communication skills also supports you to progress into leadership roles within data-driven organisations. Where have previous Applied Data Science (Conversion) graduates worked? Previous graduates from this course have gone on to a range of roles, including: Data Scientist at NHS Arden and GEM CSU Data Analyst at Hilbrix Data Scientist at Twinkl Educational Publishing Data and Insights Manager at Adam Smith Institute AI Research & Product Development at Pathway AI Consulting Research Assistant at ARU Data Quality and Insights Analyst at National Energy System Operator Senior Data Analyst at Pay.UK How can ARU help with my employability and career development? We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning which may include industry-led projects, placements or Professional Experience modules . Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules There are many paths to becoming a data scientist. What matters is curiosity, commitment and a willingness to learn and explore. Dr Mahdi Maktabdar Oghaz, Course Leader Develop the knowledge and practical skills needed to become a confident data scientist, whatever your previous academic background. You'll begin by building strong foundations through Analytical Techniques and Programming with Python, before progressing to Principles of Data Mining and Machine Learning, where you'll develop predictive models and extract meaningful insights from real-world data. In Applied Data Analysis and Research Methodology, you'll learn to analyse complex datasets using industry-standard tools and apply robust research methods to data-driven investigations. The course culminates in the Data Analytics Major Project, where you'll independently apply the knowledge and skills gained throughout the programme to solve a real-world problem in a domain of your choice. What will I study? Modules are subject to change and availability, and may vary by location. If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. London, our Public Health course equips students with the skills to deliver evidence-based solutions to today’s health challenges, improve population health, and strengthen healthcare systems in the UK and around the world” Overview Structure and content Entry requirements Teaching and assessment Employability Course Fees Course Aims Course Learning Outcomes Overview The Master of Public Health (MPH) at ARU London is designed to prepare students for careers focused on improving health and wellbeing at a population level. Centred around the key principles of health protection, health improvement, and service development, the course provides a thorough understanding of the social, economic, environmental, and political factors that influence health outcomes in diverse communities. London’s unique setting offers students a valuable opportunity to study public health issues within a live and varied urban environment. You will develop core skills in research, critical analysis, leadership, and communication while gaining experience in assessing health needs, planning interventions, and evaluating outcomes. The course explores real-world public health challenges using case studies and applied learning, and incorporates current thinking around sustainability, ethical practice, global citizenship, and inclusive care. With input from public health professionals and sector experts, the course content remains closely aligned with the needs of employers and evolving industry expectations. The programme includes a final major project where you will apply your learning to a real or simulated public health issue, allowing you to demonstrate your knowledge, practical ability, and strategic thinking. By the end of the course, you will be equipped to pursue a range of roles within local authorities, NHS and international organisations, NGOs, and public policy teams, or to continue your studies in a specialised or management-focused direction. Structure and content Over the course of your masters, you will study a total of 6 modules. See below for the modules which you will study: Postgraduate Study Skills, Research Methods, and Ethics (Healthcare) This module supports your transition to postgraduate study by developing essential academic and research skills. You will learn how to design research projects, analyse healthcare data, and understand ethical principles in public health research. Determinants of Population Health Explore the social, economic, environmental, and political factors that influence population health. This module focuses on understanding health inequalities and how public health professionals can address them. Health Protection Learn how to assess and manage risks to public health, including communicable diseases, environmental hazards, and emergency planning. The module also covers surveillance systems and health risk communication. Finance and Governance in Health and Social Care Examine how financial management, regulation, and governance structures impact health and social care delivery. You will gain insights into policy frameworks, accountability, and funding in public health systems. Population Healthcare and Health Improvement Focus on the planning, delivery, and evaluation of health improvement programmes across communities. You will learn to apply evidence-based approaches to influence health behaviours and improve outcomes. Postgraduate Major Project (Healthcare) Apply your knowledge to a substantial, independent project focused on a real-world public health issue. This capstone module allows you to design and complete research, evaluate findings, and demonstrate your critical and analytical abilities. These are delivered across three trimesters in full-time or part-time formats, with September, January, and May intakes available. This course uses a blend of classroom teaching, case studies, experiential learning, and practical assignments. Learning methods include: Team-based and problem-solving exercises Interactive lectures and debates Guest sessions with public health professionals Simulation activities and case study analysis Capstone project grounded in real-life public health issues From the beginning, your learning will be linked to your career aspirations, with professional and academic guidance to help you chart your path in public health. For a more detailed overview of the course modules you can view the Course Information Sheet here . Teaching and assessment You will learn through a variety of teaching methods including lectures, seminars, group work, simulations, and case study analysis. Learning is interactive and practice-focused, giving you opportunities to apply principles to real-life scenarios. Timetable Full-time Schedule: Standard delivery Studying on campus 2 days a week which is Monday - Friday (10:00-17:00) Non-Standard delivery (Available for September intakes only) Evening and weekend delivery: Our non-standard delivery is on a Tuesday + Thursday evening (18:00 to 21:00) + Saturday (10:00 to 17:00) Part-time Schedule: Standard delivery Studying on campus 1 day a week which is Monday - Friday (10:00-17:00) Assessment ARU London employs assessments that are designed to measure student progress, and to reflect professional practice work. Assignments include, but are not limited to: Written coursework: these offer the student the opportunity to develop and demonstrate skills to communicate in written form, to different audiences Oral presentations these offer the student the opportunity to develop and demonstrate ability to communicate orally, to different audiences Examinations: these offer the student the opportunity to develop and demonstrate ability to work within strict time constraints Examinations, in-class tests and online quizzes: these offer the student the opportunity to develop and demonstrate ability to work within strict time constraints and, in relation to the latter, to feedback on their ongoing learning Practical projects and reflective work: these offer the student the opportunity to develop and demonstrate independent practice and personal growth through reflection A final major project or dissertation: this offers the student the opportunity to demonstrate advanced academicism through conducting detailed research, analysis and reporting of an issue of personal academic or professional practice interest. The Major Project is based on an organisation selected by the candidate in discussion with their project supervisor. Employability Graduates of the MPH will be well-prepared for a wide range of public health roles in local, national, and international organisations. Possible career paths include roles such as public health analysts, health promotion specialists, policy advisors, and global health consultants. Students with entrepreneurial aspirations will also have the opportunity to be supported in exploring and growing their own ventures, such as exploring the roles of independent consultancy in public health. The Enterprise Hub is a dedicated group within the university offering adivce and support for helping students start or grow their own independent buisnesses. Potential employers include: Local authorities NHS public health teams Charities and NGOs such as Save the Children or the Red Cross International organisations like the World Health Organization (WHO) or UNESCO Policy think tanks Academic and research institutions The course equips students with transferable skills in research, critical thinking, and communication, and offers career support services including CV workshops and interview preparation. The capstone Major Project allows students to engage with real-world challenges, further strengthening their professional portfolio. Manage practical public health challenges through the application of appropriate skills and theoretical knowledge. Think and act as a global citizen, with a focus on appropriate ethical approaches and futureproofing to deliver public health sustainability. Evaluate, synthesise, and utilise the varied information available to and for public health, and develop appropriate research frameworks for collecting and critically analysing public health information Appraise and evaluate theories for the management of resources to deliver public health and develop methods of sustaining and improving those resources. Understand, evaluate, and utilise appropriate theoretical frameworks related to public health interventions. Solve complex public health problems and make decisions through appropriate problem definition, research planning, analysis, and evaluation. Gain a thorough insight into contemporary research and leading-edge practice within the field of public health. Foster innovation, creativity, and generate originality and enterprise in approaching complex public health issues. Demonstrate self-direction and autonomy in research and scholarship and continue to advance knowledge and understanding, and master new skills to postgraduate level. Course Learning Outcomes Knowledge and Understanding Understanding and Application of Public Health Knowledge Graduates will critically evaluate the complex, dynamic nature of public health shaped by individual, societal, environmental, and global contexts, using contemporary theories and advanced scholarship to investigate and resolve public health challenges (A01, A02, A03). Research and Strategy Development They will synthesise diverse information sources to design population-appropriate strategies and interventions, while critically appraising research methods and applying them to contemporary public health issues (A04, A10). Technology, Communication, and Innovation Graduates will understand and evaluate the role of evolving technologies, including AI, in driving public health intelligence and innovation, and recognise the importance of entrepreneurship and creativity in advancing public health practice (A05, A09). Cultural, Ethical, and Global Perspectives They will assess the impact of DEIA and cultural differences, navigate cross-cultural challenges, and address globalisation and ethical dilemmas in the planning and delivery of public health interventions (A06, A07, A08). Intellectual (thinking), practical, affective and transferrable skills Critical Thinking, Communication, and Problem Solving Graduates will think critically and creatively, challenge assumptions, and communicate complex ideas clearly to diverse audiences. They will solve real-world public health problems through rigorous data synthesis, research, and application of theory to practice (B01, B02, B03, B04). Diversity, Collaboration, and Practice They will demonstrate awareness of DEIA principles in public health delivery, work collaboratively in interprofessional settings, and effectively manage group dynamics and tasks (B05, B06). Operational Competence and Professional Growth Graduates will manage risk, resources, and funding in public health projects, using information effectively. They will also engage in critical self-reflection, manage ethical dilemmas, and evaluate policy impacts while developing their professional practice (B07, B08, B09). Autonomy and Global Citizenship They will act with autonomy in learning and practice, apply knowledge to improve public health outcomes, and operate with a commitment to social justice, environmental stewardship, and global awareness (B10). Undergraduate BSc (Hons) Nursing (Mental Health) Empower and support patients in their journey to recovery with our NMC-validated Mental Health Nursing degree course. Our course pages need JavaScript enabled to work correctly. Apply by 25 September Mental health nursing is a challenging but rewarding field. As a qualified nurse, you’ll identify sometimes vulnerable people’s needs, plan and provide care, and encourage them to believe that recovery is possible. This accredited course mixes quality classroom teaching with hands-on placements . As well as developing your practical skills, you’ll learn about causes and interventions; the experiences of people from different demographics and backgrounds; and biological, psychological and social factors that can impact on mental health. When you graduate, you’ll have the skills and knowledge you need to start your nursing career. Nursing & Midwifery Council Our Nursing degree courses are validated by the NMC and you’ll be linked to one of our eight NHS healthcare trust partners for your placements. This is ARU Nursing students speaking for themselves — no filter, just an honest take on what the course is really like. Close full-screen gallery. This is ARU Nursing students speaking for themselves — no filter, just an honest take on what the course is really like. Why ARU? Gain clinical experience with placements in diverse mental health settings. Learn from professionals with backgrounds in mental health nursing. Train in cutting-edge simulation suites and clinical skills labs. Study an NMC-approved course that ensures professional standards. Get a minimum of £5,000 per year non-repayable training grant. Benefit from comprehensive support services including careers, wellbeing, and academic guidance. Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers "Once you're qualified, it really opens your eyes to the mass of opportunities that are available, like working for the Ministry of Justice, GP primary care services or in clinical education." Will, Mental Health Nursing graduate As a graduate, you'll be prepared for professional practice. Our course is approved by the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) in the UK, meaning you’ll be eligible to apply for registration with them when you graduate – and start your career in mental health nursing. You might choose to work in settings such as in-patient care, home treatment, or a community mental health team. Over 90% of our students have gone on to work or study, 15 months after their course (source: Discover Uni ). What can you do with a mental health nursing degree? As a registered nurse you’ll be able to work in a variety of job roles and settings. There are also several well-established ways to progress in your career. You could become a nurse specialist with expertise in (for example) working with children or older people, with specific interventions such as talking therapies, or in specific settings such as drug or alcohol treatment services. Or you could become an advanced clinical practitioner or even a nurse consultant, dedicating part of your time to research or improving best practice. Another opportunity for progression is as a nurse leader, for example a ward manager in a hospital who leads a team of nurses and other professionals. Alternatively, you might help to develop mental health services, or influence healthcare policy. Some nurses also become a nurse educator, developing and supporting the next generation of healthcare professionals. Alternatively, you could take your education further with a post-registration course, conduct research or go into healthcare management . Supporting people with their recovery ARU graduate Henry works as a community mental health nurse. He's become involved in research, as well as the development of support surrounding autistic spectrum conditions. Teaching and modules This is a highly practical course and you'll go on placements from Year 1. You'll start by completing two hospital placements and building your confidence around the safe administration of medication. You'll also look at person-centred care and the nature of mental illness, and learn about ethical theories and legal principles relating to mental health. What will I study? If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. Year 1 Into ARU Foundations of Communication and Professionalismfor Nursing Fundamental Skills and Procedures for Nursing Applied Health Science for Nursing Across the Lifespan Epidemiology, Inequality, and Health Promotion for Nursing Across the Lifespan Contemporary Nursing Practice 1 Year 2 Supporting a Patient Safety Culture in Nursing Supporting Learning and Professional Development in Nursing Contemporary Nursing Practice 2 Assessing and Planning Care Across the Lifespan Coordinating and Leading Integrated Care in Interprofessional Settings Year 3 Assessment in Mental Health Nursing Developing Approaches to Planning Care in Mental Health Nursing Contemporary Mental Health Nursing Practice 3 Reviewing and Evaluating Mental Health Nursing Care Therapeutic Interventions in Mental Health Nursing Module details With foundation year To prepare you for university study, you can take a foundation year at the start of this course. Find out more about foundation years . Year 1 Core Maths Biology: Physiology Preparing for a Career in Caring Learning to Learn Psychology Embracing Diversity Health and Wellbeing Module details March start You can start this course in March, in Chelmsford. You'll study the same modules as students who start in September (including a foundation year, if you choose this option). What happens during placements? Our mental health nursing degree places equal value on clinical practice and theory – and you’ll spend 50% of your learning time on placement. You’ll be required to have DBS and occupational health clearance, including all your vaccinations, and to have completed all mandatory training and induction sessions before you can go on placement. Placements are a great chance to get hands-on experience in providing nursing care, and assessing, treating and communicating with patients. You may find yourself working at a GP surgery; in a variety of hospital settings, from A&E through to acute care and oncology; or working with a community team. With services being delivered remotely, we have placements integrating digital health and with virtual wards and teams. We also have virtual placements, where you can focus on the fundamental elements of nursing care in a safe, supportive environment, but access this from a home computer. Some virtual placements are delivered by practice partners, who work with us to ensure that the placement develops your knowledge and skills, and provides time for reflection and active discussion. Other virtual placements are delivered by ARU staff. Each placement lasts around 4 - 10 weeks and you will have experience in both the acute and community settings during the course. There are opportunities in older person care, dementia care, community nursing, social care, surgical and medical setting, virtual wards and more. There’s also the option of a self-funded overseas placement at the end of Year 2. While on placement, you’ll be working shifts, averaging 37.5 hours per week. This can mean early, late and night shifts, as well as weekends and bank holidays. You’ll be supported by practice supervisors and assessors as well as staff from ARU. You’ll be required to follow the uniform policy at University and on placement. In many clinical areas, in order to minimise the risk of infection, clothing is not permitted below the elbows. Please talk to one of our tutors about this if you have questions or would like more information. We’ll expect you to provide personal care to male, female and transgender patients. Each year, you’ll get allocated annual leave at set points to support you in balancing your course and relaxation time. These weeks may not coincide with school holidays. Our placement maps will help you plan your travel before you start on the course. What will I learn on placement? We want to make sure you experience a variety of placements and that you graduate as an effective practitioner. To meet the NMC standards, you will require practice learning opportunities to enable you to develop the skills to deliver safe and effective care to a diverse range of people. Nurses must be able to care for people in their own home, in the community or hospital or any health care setting, and you will experience a range of placements during the course. Your learning on placement will cover the required platforms: Being an accountable professional Promoting health and preventing ill health Assessing needs and planning care Providing and evaluating care Leading and managing nursing care and working in teams Improving safety and quality of care Coordinating care You will also gain experience in the required communication and relationship management skills, and nursing procedures. Examples of nursing procedures include: Undertaking a history and accurately assess people of all ages. Undertaking a whole-body systems assessment including respiratory, circulatory, neurological, musculoskeletal, cardiovascular and skin status. Assessing mental and physical health and wellbeing status Undertake venepuncture and cannulation and blood sampling, interpreting normal and common abnormal blood profiles and venous blood gases. Undertake chest auscultation and interpret findings Use of contemporary nutritional assessment tools Managing the administration of IV fluids Observe, assess and respond to potential infection risks using best practice guidelines Assess and review preferences and care priorities of the dying person and their family and carers Exercise professional accountability in ensuring the safe administration of medicines to those receiving care Where will I go on placements? You’ll be linked to one of our NHS healthcare trust partners for your placements, and have additional placements virtually or in health and social care settings. If you study in Cambridge, your clinical placements will be with in-patient services and community specialists across south, mid and north Cambridgeshire. If you study in Chelmsford, your clinical placements will be with in-patient services and community specialists across Essex. There’s also the option of a self-funded overseas placement with Work the World during Year 2. We make every effort to minimise the travelling distance involved but you may have to travel some distance to your placement. It is your responsibility to plan your journey and make sure you are on time for your shifts. Placement maps Nursing placements take place in these areas, depending on the nursing subject you choose and the campus you study at. Adult and Child Nursing - Essex Mental Health Nursing - Essex Adult and Child Nursing – Cambridgeshire Mental Health Nursing – Cambridgeshire How is Nursing (Mental Health) assessed? To make sure you’re developing the skills and knowledge needed for professional practice, we use a range of assessment methods. These include essays, presentations, exams, case studies, project work and assessment of practice competencies in the clinical setting. We know feedback is essential for your progress and our lecturers take pride in giving you clear guidance on how to improve your expertise. What equipment will I need? Books An electronic tablet to access course content and undertake assessment in the practice setting Sensible shoes (as per uniform policy) Fob watch Who teaches Nursing (Mental Health) at ARU? At ARU, you’ll learn in small, supportive group sessions led by our highly experienced staff. They’ll also offer support while you’re on placement, along with your practice supervisors and assessors. You’ll use sophisticated equipment to simulate many aspects of a working hospital ward. You’ll also learn from registered, practising tutors and lecturers who’ll make sure you’re being taught the latest techniques and give you the support you need to succeed. Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust/IDC (Industrial Diagnostics Company) will undertake the vaccinations on behalf of ARU. Please also be aware that if you were to catch either Covid or flu during your course, it may result in significant disruption to your studies. Postgraduate MSc Child and Adolescent Mental Wellbeing Get the knowledge and understanding you need to manage young people’s mental wellbeing. Study with us by distance learning. Source: Graduate Outcomes Survey 2026 According to the Mental Health Foundation , 10% of five- to 16-year-olds have a diagnosable mental health problem. Prevalence can increase with age, highlighting the importance of early intervention. On this specialist Masters degree, you’ll explore children’s psychological development and learn about interventions and treatment. If you have a degree-level qualification and a strong interest child and adolescent mental health, we welcome your application. You don’t need to be working in healthcare or mental health to apply. Why ARU? Join this course if you have experience in healthcare, or are new to the field Explore social and cultural influences on mental health and wellbeing Develop your knowledge of interventions and treatments Choose to study full- or part-time by distance learning Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers Strengthen your employment opportunities in the areas of health, social care and education. You’ll graduate with an expert understanding of mental wellbeing issues affecting children and adolescents – and a range of skills that employers value. There's growing demand for child and adolescent mental health practitioners, and you’ll find opportunities across the public and private sectors. What can you do with a Child and Adolescent Mental Wellbeing degree? Child and adolescent mental health experts work in a range of settings related to health, social care and education. Roles may include children’s mental health adviser, ambassador, or research assistant. Graduation doesn’t have to be the end of your time with us. You might choose to embark on a postgraduate research programme, such as our Professional Doctorate in Health and Social Care . How can ARU help with my employability and career development? We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning which may include industry-led projects, placements or Professional Experience modules . Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules Develop a comprehensive understanding of the mental health conditions that children may be diagnosed with – and how they can best be supported. You’ll focus on the significance of psyche development on mental health, and explore areas including language and cognitive development, social communication, behaviour regulation, learning disabilities, and coping mechanisms. To gain a holistic understanding of children’s mental wellbeing, you’ll also explore cultural, social and family influences. Finally, you’ll complete a Major Project. This is an opportunity to carry out research into an area of specific interest to you. What will I study? Jump to a section Introduction Course options Key facts Teaching and assessment Entry requirements Fees and paying for university Facilities Accreditation Careers Introduction Develop your knowledge of sustainable practices, new technologies, science and research to produce plants and crops, with our MSc Horticulture at ARU Writtle. Horticulture encompasses a diverse range of activities – from landscaping to production of food and non-food crops. With population growth and climate change impacting upon production, it’s vital to investigate new growing systems and establish crops which can be grown sustainably and transported to market with minimal losses. As a student at ARU Writtle you’ll have access to a research glasshouse, our campus farm and the Postharvest Unit, which undertakes research and trials with commercial companies. We’ll also arrange visits to growers and post-harvest facilities. This gives you the opportunity to study a range of crops and develop an understanding of postharvest handling. On campus, you’ll hear from visiting speakers and build your awareness of the latest trends and research in industry. There are opportunities to specialise as the course progresses, with a range of optional modules. Our Masters degree is ideal if you want to develop your knowledge of horticulture and take the next step in your career. Read more Study your postgraduate degree at ARU and gain an advanced level of knowledge and skills to enhance your career prospects. We offer practical, industry-focused courses that are informed by staff expertise, our sector links, and the latest research. Our MSc Horticulture is taught at Writtle , a friendly and welcoming campus set in the beautiful Essex countryside, just two miles from Chelmsford with its excellent train links to London and East Anglia. ","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Applied Research (Methods) for Managers (15 credits)","Description":"The module introduces research and research methods from the perspectives of the researcher, research manager or managerial user and gives them the opportunity to deepen more into areas of their preference. The module will discuss the research process of: identifying issues and problems; specifying research; systematic design, collecting and processing primary and secondary data and information; analysing findings using quantitative and qualitative approaches and producing conclusions, recommendations and suggestions for further investigation. Emphasis will be placed on methods that are objective, systematic, reliable, valid, ethical, effective and efficient. Guidance will also be given on the preparation of research papers and reports. Taught postgraduates from all disciplines will initially share a generic overview that is appropriate for a postgraduate understanding of research and the methods that underpin it. Thereafter, you will apply principles of research in a more contextualised approach according to their discipline. You will have the opportunity to experience the whole journey of applied research to provide answers to real-life issues in food systems- from research design to dissemination to a wide audience.","Code":"MOD011221","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"4baa6f60-549d-4267-bfc1-9e8ee07f8a75"},{"Title":"Food Security and Sustainable Agriculture (15 credits)","Description":"This module presents current scientific theory in sustainable farm land management and competitive food production with a specific reference to agricultural ecology and ecosystem resilience. Sustainable land management and food security requires innovative, risk-robust strategies to meet growing demands in the future and to ensure ecosystems remain fully functional and resilient to uncertain changes. You will be able to analyse and critically evaluate current policy and strategies practiced in the UK and the wider global sphere through a review of case studies. Applications of new scientific thinking and technology will be observed. The aim of the module is to provide you with the latest applied scientific theory in sustainable farming practices, agricultural ecology and food production.","Code":"","HideMdfLink":true,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"018c8455-92b0-4ccf-942a-2f98e0eef9d3"}],"OptionalModules":[{"Title":"Sustainable Crop Production A (15 credits)","Description":"During this module, you'll evaluate the factors which determine the level and location of crop production in relation to climate and agro-economic factors, using a number of crop examples related to horticulture, and agriculture. The development and changing patterns of cropping systems and production techniques will be discussed in the light of changing market requirements, need for continuity of supply, environmental pressures and the need for sustainability in production. The importance of global trade will be considered in terms of sustainability and environmental footprint; other environmental considerations such as energy consumption and use of non-renewable resources that of increasing importance to industry will be considered as part of the crop production process. Current research and trends will be evaluated and likely future developments considered.","Code":"","HideMdfLink":true,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"7b94fad2-5db5-43ed-b7fc-751158b48f72"},{"Title":"Postharvest Systems Management A (15 credits)","Description":"Fresh produce is nutritionally important to human diet, but such produce is often highly perishable and susceptible to loss. This food also supports interest in plant-based eating patterns and shifts in dietary choices. This module will examine the role of postharvest practice and the challenges it faces in maintaining the quality of fresh produce across supply chains. Such knowledge is also seen as a means of reducing food loss and waste, improving food security and tackling global hunger. Managing the quality of fresh produce through postharvest practice requires an understanding of postharvest biology, both the biotic and abiotic causes of deterioration and the connections to preharvest production. This knowledge will be used to evaluate current postharvest methods, challenges and potential solutions to meet changing needs and extend shelf life. The module will familiarise you with key qualitative and quantitative parameters used to assess quality attributes, examining current and future techniques that mitigate postharvest loss and deterioration and meet consumers’ needs. You will be encouraged to problem solve and acquire and build on knowledge sequentially using flexible delivery linked to learning outcomes.","Code":"","HideMdfLink":true,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"7d5be28f-e3f7-4215-a8ae-56eaea241c6d"},{"Title":"Sustainable Crop Production B (15 credits)","Description":"Based on the what has been discussed in the module Sustainable Crop Production A, you will discuss in more detail the international basis for revealing the underlying mechanisms of sustainable cropping systems to drive agronomic innovations. Sustainable cropping elements will be discussed in more depth with greater focus on novel scientific findings on improvement in cropping systems related to crop yields and their resistance to biotic and abiotic stressors, resource use efficiency, environmental impact, sustainability, and ecosystem services.","Code":"","HideMdfLink":true,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"ead794ce-b2dd-44b8-a96a-4fc3c143e8ab"},{"Title":"Postharvest Systems Management B (15 credits)","Description":"Reducing food loss and waste today is an urgent and pressing challenge with the UN Secretary General calling it 'an ethical outrage'. Future food demands and food security will require intensified sustainable production but also necessitate a reduction of this food loss and waste across the value chain. The FAO estimates that 14% of global production is lost each year after harvest before reaching the market through postharvest loss and waste. This is estimated to equate to approximately 38% of total energy in the global food system. The maintenance and modification of crop quality after harvest is particularly important to fresh produce which is notoriously perishable and susceptible to loss. This module examines the potential issues and solutions to reducing loss and waste across the supply chain, including at the retail and consumer level through to redistribution. Such loss will be examined in the context of consumer behaviour and sustainable and environmental pressures. Production methods and postharvest biology in relation to short and long supply chains, will be used to explore the key contributory factors that affect quality. The module will allow you to become familiar with key analytical techniques used to assess quality attributes and will examine current and future techniques and technologies that have the potential to mitigate postharvest loss and deterioration. This will draw on an understanding of quality in relation to postharvest physiology and shelf life. You'll be encouraged to focus on crop(s) or technologies of their choice and develop their own analytical approach to solving a simulated or real-life postharvest problem. An understanding of the causes of loss from farm, retail, food service through to that at the household level will be needed in relation to different food systems. Factors such as handling, transport and storage, cold chain capacity and packaging will be linked to consumer trends and knowledge in the overarching aim of environmental sustainability and pressures on land and resources. You will be encouraged to explore business models to reduce postharvest loss, including cost barriers, in the context of waste reduction, short and long value chains drawing on examples from importers, quality and produce managers. Current innovations to improve postharvest quality and/or nutritional value will be examined. Cross- modular thinking will be encouraged to consolidate systems thinking competency to assess problems and drivers of constructive change.","Code":"","HideMdfLink":true,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"c52bf8b6-c0ea-49ac-89a2-35505c449361"},{"Title":"Other Level 7 module by negotiation with the course team (15 credits)","Description":"","Code":"","HideMdfLink":true,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"e313a43e-be2c-44ad-8d09-0ddf707232b4"}],"Id":"c5bf92e0-50fa-428b-b8cb-719e63295cfb","SelectedModule":false},{"Title":"Year 2","CoreModuleSectionHeading":"","OptionModuleSectionHeading":"Optional modules","Summary":"

","CoreModules":[],"OptionalModules":[{"Title":"Sustainable Global Business Management and Circular Economics (15 credits)","Description":"The aim of this module is to explore the sustainable use of resources and how better management of the factors of production can lead to both a competitive advantage and sustainable resource use outcome. Today, the linearity of the global economy is becoming hard to escape; excess waste piled in landfills and littered along coastlines are visible hallmarks of a “take, make, dispose” paradigm fuelled by business and devoured by consumers. Despite such worrying trends, the linear model is still going strong and continues to form the basis of much of today's production and consumption patterns. In fact, only 9% of primary resources, which include biomass, fossil fuels, metals, and non-metallic minerals, are being circulated in some form. Linear systems are easier to understand, model and manage. You will consider how businesses decide on the combinations of inputs to produce their desired output/s within the limits of sustainable systems. The changing dynamics affecting these choices will be analysed. The raised awareness over the social impacts of these choices will be considered. How are businesses altering their resource allocation decisions in light of better understanding of the environmental costs, coupled with increased customer demand for such changes? In the past ownership of resources was a major source of power. Today it is the sustainable management of such scarce items that is becoming increasingly important. This coupled with consumer demand and Government regulation is impacting how businesses operate.","Code":"MOD011224","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"81d8d596-b005-499e-98ee-9c8ffbcc45b9"},{"Title":"Experiential Learning A (30 credits)","Description":"This module is designed to help you review or improve your professional practice. You will operate with a high level of autonomy to work upon a work-based or sector-based problem, and to apply knowledge and techniques at the forefront of your discipline in an area of professional practice. You will be required to evaluate critically current scholarship and work-based practices and to use your knowledge to either: a) provide a critical review of a work-based problem and suggest possible ways forward, or b) implement and investigate novel and creative solutions to a problem. In keeping with the flexible and individualised approach to learning, you will have the opportunity to identify and choose suitable Level 7 projects and problems within your sector that contribute to your career role, skills development and career aspirations. We may be able to guide you towards suitable projects, depending on availability and external collaboration and will approve such projects at concept, supporting you through to completion. The work carried out in this module will be separate to but can be broadly linked to research interests defined through the approved dissertation topic. The agreed pattern, intensity of delivery and the format of the output case study is flexible to suit the workplace and individual’s needs but will be agreed at project concept to ensure it satisfies course outcomes.","Code":"","HideMdfLink":true,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"caf3d675-0bd4-4f19-9159-0e5d20c957b3"},{"Title":"Experiential Learning B (15 credits)","Description":"This module is designed to help you review or improve your professional practice. You will operate with a high level of autonomy to work upon a work-based problem or sector-based problem or gaps in understanding and to apply knowledge and techniques at the forefront of your discipline in an area of professional practice. You will be required to evaluate critically current scholarship and work-based practices and to use your knowledge to either: a) provide a critical review of a work-based problem and suggest possible ways forward, or b) implement and investigate novel and creative solutions to a problem. In keeping with the flexible approach to learning, you will have the opportunity to identify refine and complete work on a suitable Level 7 project and /or problems within your sector that contribute to your role, career or skills aspirations. We may be able to guide you towards suitable projects, depending on availability. There may be opportunities to base this module at a Higher Education Institution or research organisation abroad, subject to agreement on quality assurance. The work carried out in this module will be a separate discrete unit of study but may be broadly linked to research to be conducted for the approved Dissertation topic. Agreement on the output will be made at project approval to offer direct relevance to the workplace but will need to satisfy level and course outcomes. Therefore, this 30-credit module can be taken in semester A, but the pattern and intensity of delivery and study can be adapted to suit your employment needs and/or industry and sector interests, reflecting the independent Level 7 study such pre-approved individualised learning provides.","Code":"","HideMdfLink":true,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"de78f94d-92c5-4c80-9ca5-ab00e58f36df"},{"Title":"Strategic Management (15 credits)","Description":"This module will enable you to understand the economic and political environment in which an arable or horticultural business operates and to develop a flexible, pragmatic approach to management based on strategic concepts and theories. Key approaches to strategy through analysis, choice, implementation and enterprise assessment will be evaluated. Options will be assessed using current case studies and materials enabling the preparation of relevant and applied business plans. These will be based on an understanding of the processes of management that are essential to both agricultural and horticultural businesses.","Code":"MOD011219","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"81b3412b-2f9a-473f-8188-1eaaf43d6ebc"},{"Title":"Sustainable Land Stewardship and Leadership (15 credits)","Description":"Used in the context of natural resources, the term stewardship means, in its broadest sense, people taking care of the earth. Sustainable land stewardship is a strategy designed to protect the natural environment in all forms of managed rural landscapes, including agriculture, forestry and non-productive green infrastructure. The approach adopted is participatory, involving landowners and users and with the support of a wide range of civil society groups. Through the implementation of voluntary agreements between landowners/users and land stewardship organisations, nature, biodiversity, ecological integrity and landscape, values will be maintained and restored. The methods employed generally focus on encouraging landowners, individuals and families, businesses, municipalities and other organisations and users (e.g. farmers, hunters, fishers) to transition from traditional practices towards systems that restore and recover natural attributes fundamental for the effective functioning of ecosystems. Without these, the services and benefits derived from healthy ecosystems are greatly diminished and will ultimately impact on human well-being. Though stewardship tools may be employed to restrict the use of specific ecologically sensitive (biodiversity-rich) areas, they also are used to restrict certain practices such as intensive agricultural, forestry or amenity practices or to maintain or restore others (e.g. extensive agriculture, use of ecologically sensitive lands). A stewardship approach is distinct from strictly protected area management as the intention is to maintain productivity within ecologically defined boundaries of acceptable operation. In this module you will apply theories and principles of systems thinking, circular economics and regenerative land use practices within the rural landscape, particularly, in agriculture and forestry.","Code":"","HideMdfLink":true,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"44bd8799-55a7-4122-87bb-54a76734084f"},{"Title":"Other Level 7 module by negotiation with the course team (15 credits)","Description":"","Code":"","HideMdfLink":true,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"e313a43e-be2c-44ad-8d09-0ddf707232b4"}],"Id":"dafdb140-2677-459e-a9a1-6729d8649f15","SelectedModule":false},{"Title":"Year 3","CoreModuleSectionHeading":"Core modules","OptionModuleSectionHeading":"","Summary":"

Undergraduate BA (Hons) Politics and International Relations Study the workings of society and governments around the globe, including questions of power, justice, democracy, empire, security, revolution, activism, and identity. Our course pages need JavaScript enabled to work correctly. Source: GOS 2026 Gain insights into change and continuity in national and global governance, how leaders and politicians have influenced such processes, and how the directions and decisions of political parties and institutions affect people’s lives. You’ll explore the impact of individual leaders like Tony Blair and Vladimir Putin alongside the role of international organisations and alliances. With a curriculum that stretches across Africa, Asia and Europe, you'll also look at wider issues of international conflict and world peace, consumption and trade, crime and terrorism, and media and communication. Find out more about studying Politics and International Relations at ARU. Close full-screen gallery. Find out more about studying Politics and International Relations at ARU. Why ARU? Gain important transferable skills for your career, including research and data analysis. Take innovative assessments that include but also go beyond the traditional essay, like blogs, podcasts, presentations and letters. Learn from expert tutors including historians, sociologists and political scientists. Attend events with key political figures organised by our Labour History Research Unit . Study in Cambridge, with its impressive collection of museums, libraries, archives and political clubs. Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers Graduate equipped for a career in a political party, diplomacy and other areas of the civil service, or for international organisations. Your use of data analysis and different sources from government documents to focus groups, as well as our innovative assessment methods, will all give you an impressive narrative to tell prospective employers. You can also learn a language on our optional modules, boosting your employability internationally in areas such as UN conflict resolution and diplomacy. What can you do with a Politics and International Relations degree? You could go on to work in a variety of fields, including: local government charities NGOs European and international organisations and agencies. You might also explore career paths in public service, the criminal justice system, future energy policy and planning, security, negotiation and peacekeeping, or communication and media. Or you might decide to stay at ARU and study for a Masters, such as our MA International Relations or MA International Development . Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and get 20% off your fees. Where have other politics graduates worked? Natasha studied at ARU and now works on Irish policy control with the UK Civil Service. Find out what inspired her to get involved in politics, and how our course helped her. Natasha's story . How can ARU help with my employability and career development? We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning through Live Briefs , internships and placements Ruskin Modules that help develop the skills employers value. Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules Learn about the interlocking institutions that constitute politics, and explore ideological constructs that underpin political change. You’ll also get to grips with digital methods, learning valuable skills in the digital humanities. From Year 2 you’ll explore key issues like migration and war, as well as your own interests on optional modules, and build your research skills. Finally, you’ll complete an independent project on a topic of your choice, and learn methods to communicate your research, while other modules will include exploring how social media facilitates both political activists and ‘bad actors’. A foundation year prepares you for the rest of your course, and focuses on general skills such as researching and referencing, numeracy and ICT, and communication. We'll also start to look at some more subject-specific topics. What happens on a placement year? Your placement year is a chance to put everything you’ve learnt in Years 1 and 2 into practice. Spend typically 9-12 months working for an organisation, developing your skills and gaining valuable work experience. Our Placements Team is here to help you secure a placement. How is Politics and International Relations assessed? You’ll show your progress through a combination of traditional essays and exams as well as more innovative methods that reflect skills you’ll need for the workplace, including blogs, podcasts, live briefs, portfolios, presentations, data collection and letters. We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning through Live Briefs , internships and placements Ruskin Modules that help develop the skills employers value. Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules We’ll start by focussing on human development and the role played by parents and other key people in children’s lives, as well as your own development as a learner. Later, we’ll consider wider and more complex issues around children’s education, including children’s rights and protection, and disability, difference and special educational needs. In your final year, you’ll also explore leadership and management, and complete an independent research project on a relevant topic of your choice. Throughout the course you’ll gain experience on placement, and achieve your Early Childhood Practitioner Competencies. What will I study? BA (Hons) 3 years full-time distance learning Top-up - distance learning BA (Hons) This course is an accelerated degree by hybrid learning, meaning it takes place over 2 years instead of 3 years, and you can study in your own time, around other commitments such as your job, children or hobbies. You’ll join us on campus for 3 full days each trimester with your tutors and peers, attending workshops and guest lectures to compliment your studies. Our learning management system, Canvas, will give you access to a comprehensive range of study resources and allow you to take part in optional online workshops with the Course Director. Our expert tutors will be on hand to offer advice and regular feedback, too. Our accelerated degree can save over £5,000 on tuition fees plus any living costs. See more information about the distance learning top up on our distance learning website . What are the teaching times? You have the option to study this course over three years by distance learning, or as an accelerated degree over two years by blended learning. Distance learning allows you to study entirely remotely, with online drop-in tutor sessions during three weeks per trimester. Blended learning is largely remote, with three full-day face-to-face teaching sessions in Chelmsford per year. Dates are subject to change, but usually these sessions are in weeks 2, 7 and 11 of each trimester. Find out more about accelerated learning and blended learning with our blog posts. What happens during a placement? Placements can help you hone your skills and get hands-on practical experience. You’ll complete 80 days during your course (25 days if you're studying the top-up). Our Practice Development Tutors will be on hand to help you find a placement, but you should aim to have this in place from the beginning of the course. If you study by distance learning and are already working in a relevant environment, you can usually complete placement days with your current employer. Will I gain recognised Competencies? When you study with us, you’ll complete the ECGPC (Early Childhood Graduate Practitioner Competencies). This is a professionally recognised framework that’ll enhance your employability and provide clarity for employers about the graduate level of your achievements. These competencies are included on the QAA Early Childhood Studies Subject Benchmark Statements with practice at Level 6 recognised by the Department for Education (DfE). You’ll meet the nine competencies through assessed observation of practice, practice-based tasks and academic assessment. Due to the placement requirements of this course, you'll need to have your own work or voluntary placement set up at the beginning of the course, in an Ofsted rated good or outstanding setting. Our Practice Development Tutors may be able to signpost you to a suitable setting if you have difficulties. To achieve the Graduate Practitioner status you'll need to have achieved Maths GCSE grade 4/C or equivalent by completion of the degree. How is Early Childhood Studies assessed? You'll show your progress through different methods that will support the professional skills you need to progress within the education sector. These include observations, patchwork texts, presentations, case studies, portfolios, posters, investigations, reports and essays. Who teaches Early Childhood Studies at ARU?
